query: If the ticket types that create the heaviest agent workload were reduced, how much would resolution time drop?

per_column.name: category_ticket_volume
per_column.rationale: Ticket count per category is a genuine, directly relevant axis for identifying which ticket types create the heaviest workload. Values are derivable by aggregating category across rows, consistent with the sample values.

per_column.name: category_avg_resolution_hours
per_column.rationale: Conceptually central to the query, but the column is degenerate: every value is 0.0. The source rows have opened_at available (not shown) and closed_at, so a real resolution time is computable, yet all values collapse to 0, indicating a broken/constant computation that misrepresents the data. Near-constant and unsupported by evidence.

per_column.name: is_heavy_workload_category
per_column.rationale: A heavy-workload flag derived from volume gives a clean grouping variable for the query. Somewhat redundant with category_ticket_volume but adds a usable threshold categorisation. Flags align with the volume samples (high-volume categories flagged 1, lower flagged 0).

per_column.name: estimated_resolution_time_hours
per_column.rationale: All values are NULL across 500 rows, providing no analytical leverage. Not affirmatively hallucinated (NULL is not a false assertion), but as a fully empty column it fails to help the resolution-time analysis it was meant to support.

judge.rationale: The volume and heavy-workload columns are well-targeted and grounded, giving real axes to identify the workload-heavy ticket types. However, the two columns that speak directly to resolution time both fail: category_avg_resolution_hours is uniformly 0.0 (broken/misleading given closed_at and opening timestamps exist) and estimated_resolution_time_hours is entirely NULL. Since the query hinges on quantifying resolution-time impact, the operator delivers the grouping side but not the outcome side.
